title: How JavaScript Runs
summary: How V8 turns JavaScript into fast machine code, how the call stack and event loop schedule your code, and how Node uses libuv to serve many requests on one thread.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between a **compiler**, an **interpreter**, and a **JIT compiler**? Which one does V8 use, and why?
questions.hint: Think of translating a whole book first vs a live interpreter, and an interpreter who writes polished translations of phrases that keep coming up.
keyPoints: A compiler translates the whole program to machine code before it runs: slow start, fast execution
An interpreter executes the program step by step without producing machine code: fast start, slower execution
A JIT starts by interpreting, profiles the running code, and compiles hot code to optimized machine code at runtime
V8 is a JIT: Ignition interprets bytecode and collects type feedback; Sparkplug/Maglev/TurboFan compile hot functions
Mentions deoptimization when runtime assumptions (like types) are violated
questions.answer:
- A **compiler** translates the whole program into machine code **before** it runs (C, Rust, Go). Startup takes longer because of the build, but the result runs very fast.
- An **interpreter** reads and executes the program **step by step** while it runs, without producing machine code. It starts instantly but runs slower, because it re-translates the same code every time.
- A **JIT (just-in-time) compiler** does both. It starts by interpreting, **profiles** the running code (which functions are hot, which types appear), and compiles the hot code into **optimized machine code** at runtime.

**V8 is a JIT.** It parses JS into bytecode, which the **Ignition** interpreter runs while recording **type feedback** ("`a` and `b` here were always small integers"). When a function gets hot, **Sparkplug** and **Maglev** quickly compile it, and **TurboFan** builds highly optimized machine code based on those observed types.

Why: JS must **start fast** (web pages load code on the fly, no build step), but it has no type annotations, so an ahead-of-time compiler couldn't know the types. A JIT learns them by watching. The catch is **deoptimization**: if an assumption breaks, like calling `add("a", {})` after 10,000 integer calls, V8 throws the optimized code away and falls back to a slower tier.

questions.hint: Sync first. An async function runs synchronously until its first await. Then drain ALL microtasks (including ones queued while draining). Then timers in the order they were scheduled.
keyPoints: Synchronous code first: 1, 6, 8 (the async function runs until its first await)
Microtasks in queue order: 3 (first then), 7 (await continuation), then 5 (queued when the first then finished)
Microtasks queued while draining still run before any macrotask
Then macrotasks: 2 (scheduled first), then 4 (scheduled during the microtask)
Final output: 1 6 8 3 7 5 2 4
questions.answer: `1 6 8 3 7 5 2 4`. Sync: 1, 6, 8. Microtasks: `3` and `7` were queued during the script; `5` is queued when the first `.then` returns. Then timers in order: `2`, then `4`.

questions.prompt: "Node.js is single-threaded." How, then, can one Node process handle 10,000 concurrent HTTP connections? Explain the roles of V8, the event loop, libuv, the OS, and the thread pool.
questions.hint: Who does the waiting? What happens with sockets vs file reads vs password hashing?
keyPoints: Only the JavaScript runs on one thread (one call stack, run to completion); I/O waiting happens outside it
libuv provides the event loop; for sockets it uses OS readiness APIs (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) so one thread can watch thousands of connections
Work the OS can't do asynchronously (most fs calls, dns.lookup, crypto pbkdf2/scrypt, zlib) runs on libuv's thread pool, 4 threads by default
When I/O completes, callbacks are queued; the loop runs them when the stack is empty, draining microtasks between callbacks
Works well as long as each callback is short; waiting connections cost memory, not threads
questions.answer:
"Single-threaded" means only **your JavaScript** runs on one thread: one call stack, and each callback runs to completion. The **waiting** for I/O happens outside that thread.

- **V8** runs the JS: it executes callbacks quickly and returns.
- **libuv** (a C library) provides the **event loop** and async I/O.
- **The OS:** for **sockets**, libuv uses OS readiness APIs: **epoll** (Linux), **kqueue** (macOS), **IOCP** (Windows). One thread asks the kernel "tell me which of these 10,000 sockets have data", and it answers "these 7". No thread sits blocked per connection.
- **The thread pool:** some work the OS can't do asynchronously (most `fs` calls, `dns.lookup`, `crypto.pbkdf2`/`scrypt`, `zlib`) runs on libuv's pool of **4 threads by default** (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`).

When I/O finishes, its callback is **queued**. When the call stack is empty, the loop runs the next callback, and between callbacks it **drains all microtasks** (promise `.then`, code after `await`).

So 10,000 idle connections cost **memory** (a socket and some buffers, a few KB each), not 10,000 threads. If each request needs 2 ms of CPU, one process handles ~500 req/s while thousands wait on the network.

This works only while **every callback is short**. One 2-second loop blocks all 10,000 connections.

questions.prompt: After a release, p99 latency jumps from 40 ms to 3 s on **every** endpoint of a Node API, even `/health`, but CPU is only at ~25% on a 4-core machine and the database is fine. The release added a CSV export endpoint that builds the whole file in memory with a loop and `JSON.stringify`. What's happening, and how would you confirm and fix it?
questions.hint: 25% of 4 cores is exactly one core. What can't run while JS is busy?
keyPoints: The export runs long synchronous CPU work on the main thread, blocking the event loop so every other request waits
25% CPU on 4 cores = one core pegged: the single JS thread is saturated
Confirm with event-loop lag/delay metrics (e.g. perf_hooks monitorEventLoopDelay) or a CPU profile showing the export function
Fix: stream the CSV in chunks (yielding between chunks), move it to a worker thread or a background job, and run one process per core
Mentions limiting concurrency of exports or doing them asynchronously with a download link
questions.answer:
**What's happening:** the new CSV export does a long **synchronous** loop plus a huge `JSON.stringify` on the **main thread**. While that runs, the event loop is **blocked**: no other request, timer or I/O callback can run. So every endpoint, even `/health`, waits behind the export. That's why p99 jumps to ~3 s everywhere while the database looks fine.

**The 25% CPU is the clue:** 25% of 4 cores = **exactly one core pegged**. Node's single JS thread is saturated; the other three cores are idle.

**Confirm it:**

- Measure **event-loop delay** with `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()`. Normally it's a few ms; during an export it would show seconds.
- Take a **CPU profile** (`node --cpu-prof` or the inspector) during an export; the export function will dominate the flame graph.
- Correlate latency spikes with export requests in the logs.

**Fix:**

1. **Stream** the CSV: write rows in chunks to the response and yield between chunks (`await new Promise(r => setImmediate(r))`), so other requests get a turn.
2. Move it to a **worker thread** or a **background job**: return "export started", then email or show a **download link** when done.
3. **Limit concurrency** of exports (e.g. 1–2 at a time).
4. Run **one Node process per core** so one busy thread can't take down the whole machine's capacity.

questions.prompt: A login endpoint hashes passwords with `crypto.pbkdf2` (async), which takes 80 ms of CPU per hash. The server runs one Node process with the default libuv thread pool on an 8-core machine. (a) Max logins per second? (b) What if you set `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8`? (c) Why would it be a disaster to use `pbkdf2Sync` instead?
questions.hint: How many pool threads are there by default? Each can do 1 / 0.08 hashes per second.
keyPoints: (a) Default pool = 4 threads; each does 1 / 0.08 = 12.5 hashes/s, so about 50 logins/s
(b) With 8 threads on 8 cores: about 100 logins/s
Requests beyond that queue waiting for a free pool thread, raising latency
(c) pbkdf2Sync runs on the main JS thread: each login blocks the event loop for 80 ms, capping at 12.5 logins/s and freezing all other requests meanwhile
Notes the thread pool is shared with fs, dns.lookup and zlib, so slow hashing can also delay file I/O
questions.answer: (a) `4 × (1 / 0.08) = 50/s`. (b) `8 × 12.5 = 100/s`. (c) Sync hashing blocks the single JS thread: `1 / 0.08 = 12.5/s` total, and nothing else runs during each 80 ms.

questions.hint: Microtasks drain before any I/O or timer callback runs. You need a macrotask boundary, like `setImmediate`.
keyPoints: Process the array in chunks (e.g. 100k–1M items) and yield between chunks
Yield with a macrotask: await new Promise(r => setImmediate(r)) (or setTimeout), letting I/O and other requests run
await Promise.resolve() only schedules a microtask; the loop drains all microtasks before I/O, so other requests still starve
Keeps the same result by carrying h across chunks
Notes the trade-off: chunking adds total time; for heavy work prefer a worker thread
